The models are ready. The arms are ready. What is not ready is the path from a working demo to a line that runs it every shift — and that path, not the intelligence, is where programs die. A cell that ships fast but wrong stops a line for weeks; one that ships qualified disappears into it on day one.

The pace of the underlying technology is now the easy part. Manipulation models advance on a frontier that moves in months, not years — the capability that was production-ready eighteen months ago is already a generation behind, and hardware gets cheaper and more capable every quarter. If putting robots on American factory floors were a question of raw capability, it would already be done.

In this scenario it costs about $130,000 a year in loaded labor, 3,750 hours spread across a bench and an inspection table, plus around 90 burr escapes a year that reach the customer. Those figures come from published wages and stated per-part times, worked through below.
CNC capacity isn't the problem. The bottleneck is the bench behind the machines, where people break edges with hand tools and then look over every part under a lamp before it goes in the box.

, and machined housings have cleaner edges but more holes, so we went a little lower. NIST's ADACS reports cite a Pratt & Whitney estimate that 12% of machining hours went to manual deburring and chamfering.

A 12.5 kg cobot carries a radially compliant spindle and a smart camera on one tool plate. Parts arrive in two interlocked drawers, so the operator loads one while the robot works the other. The camera finds each part, then checks every edge after the pass.

The operator loads drawer B while the robot works drawer A, then they swap, and interlocks keep the robot out of the open bay. The spindle is the hazard, so the cell is fenced even with a cobot. Layout is representative.

One smart camera does two jobs. Before cutting, it reads the fixture plate code and finds each part's real position, so the path shifts to the part.
